content: A clinical trial must be conducted in compliance with Good Clinical Practice, with the protocol approved by an ethics committee before any subject is enrolled.
Informed consent must be obtained from every trial subject, or their legally acceptable representative, before any trial-related procedure is performed.
The investigator is responsible for the medical care of trial subjects and for any decisions related to their participation in the trial.
All trial-related information must be recorded, handled, and stored in a way that allows its accurate reporting, interpretation, and verification.
Source documents should be attributable, legible, contemporaneous, original, accurate, and complete.
The trial master file should be maintained at the site and be available for monitoring, audit, and inspection.
An adverse event is any untoward medical occurrence in a trial subject administered a trial product, whether or not causally related to the product.
A serious adverse event is one that results in death, is life-threatening, requires inpatient hospitalisation, causes persistent disability, or is a congenital anomaly.
DEMO PLACEHOLDER: serious adverse events must be reported to the regulator and ethics committee within 24 hours of site awareness. Verify before presenting as fact.
DEMO PLACEHOLDER: non-serious adverse events should be documented and reported within 15 days. Verify before presenting as fact.
Every adverse event narrative should include onset date, severity, seriousness criteria, action taken with the trial product, and outcome.
Causality assessment for each adverse event should be classified as related, possibly related, or not related to the trial product.
Suspected unexpected serious adverse reactions require expedited reporting in addition to the standard serious adverse event timeline.
Adverse events that are ongoing at the end of the reporting period should be followed up until resolution or stabilization.
For Ayurveda interventions, the AE narrative should document the specific formulation, batch or lot number, dose, and route of administration.
Ayurveda formulations may contain multiple botanical ingredients; the full composition should be traceable from the batch record.
Concomitant use of other Ayurvedic, Siddha, Unani, or conventional medicines must be recorded, as interactions may affect adverse event causality.
Quality control documentation for the trial formulation, including heavy metal and microbial testing, should be retained with the trial master file.
Subjects receiving Panchakarma or other procedural interventions should be monitored for procedure-related adverse events separately from product-related events.
Dietary and lifestyle regimen restrictions specified in the protocol should be documented in the subject record, since deviations may confound safety assessment.
Ethics committee approval is generally valid for one year and must be renewed before expiry for the trial to continue enrolling subjects. DEMO PLACEHOLDER.
Any protocol amendment that affects subject safety or rights must receive ethics committee approval before implementation, except where immediate action is required to protect subjects.
The ethics committee should be informed of all serious adverse events occurring at the site within the timelines defined in the approved protocol.
Compensation provisions for trial-related injury must be explained to the subject during the informed consent process.
The trial must be registered on the Clinical Trials Registry of India before the first subject is enrolled, and the registration number cited in all reports.
The CTRI record should be updated with enrolment numbers, completion dates, and posted results as the trial progresses.
Any change in the primary outcome or sample size after registration should be documented as an amendment with justification.
Site initiation visits should confirm staff training, equipment calibration, and document readiness before enrolment begins.
Monitoring visits should verify source data against case report forms and follow up on outstanding queries.
Protocol deviations should be documented, assessed for impact on subject safety and data integrity, and reported to the ethics committee where required.
A safety signal is reported information on a possible causal relationship between the trial product and an adverse event, judged worthwhile of further analysis.
Periodic safety summaries should aggregate all adverse events by severity, seriousness, and causality for review by the sponsor and investigator.
If a subject withdraws due to an adverse event, a follow-up visit should be scheduled to document resolution and any residual effects.
Continuing review of the trial by the ethics committee should occur at least annually, and more frequently for high-risk interventions.
Randomisation codes should be held securely, and unblinding procedures documented in the protocol.
Essential documents should be retained for the period required by regulation after trial completion or discontinuation.
Pregnant or breastfeeding subjects who experience adverse events require special follow-up, including outcomes for the child where relevant.
Results of the trial, including negative findings, should be posted to the registry within the required period after completion.
Storage conditions for Ayurveda trial formulations, including temperature and humidity limits, should be recorded and any excursions investigated.
Subject confidentiality must be maintained; trial data should be de-identified in reports and publications.
